title: Island Count After Each Landfill
statement:
A map of m rows and n columns starts as open water. You receive a list of landfill operations; positions[i] = [row, col] turns that cell into land.

Land cells that touch up, down, left or right belong to the same island. Diagonal contact does not connect them.

Return an array whose i-th entry is the number of islands right after operation i. A position may be filled more than once; filling a cell that is already land changes nothing.

examples.why: (1, 1) only touches the first two islands diagonally, so it starts a third one. Filling (0, 1) then joins all three at once.
The second fill hits land that already exists, so the count must not grow.
The last cell touches two cells of the same island. It merges nothing new, so the count stays at 1 instead of dropping to 0.

hints: Recounting islands with a flood fill after every operation is correct but repeats a lot of work. What actually changes when one cell becomes land?

A new cell adds one island, and then every distinct neighbouring island it touches merges into it, removing one island per merge. You need a fast way to ask "are these two cells already in the same island?".
Union-find. Give each land cell a parent pointer. On a fill, add 1, then union with each land neighbour; every union that joins two different roots subtracts 1. Path compression keeps the trees flat.

explain.intuition:
Each fill changes the count by a small, local amount. The new cell is an island of its own (+1). Then look at its four neighbours: every neighbour that is land and belongs to a different island than the new cell gets merged in, and each merge removes one island (−1). Two neighbours that are already in the same island must only count once, which is the third example.

The question "are these two cells in the same island right now?" is exactly what union-find answers. Each cell points to a parent; following parents leads to a root that names the island. Merging is one pointer change between roots. With path compression and union by size, each operation is close to O(1), so the whole run is nearly linear instead of a flood fill per step.
steps: Number cells as r · n + c. Keep parent (−1 for water), size and a running count = 0.
For each position: if it is already land, push the current count and continue.
Otherwise make it its own root and add 1 to count.
For each of the four neighbours that is land, find both roots. If they differ, link the smaller tree under the larger one and subtract 1 from count.
Push count after handling all four neighbours.
pitfalls: Counting a repeated fill as a new island. Check for existing land first.
Subtracting 1 for every land neighbour instead of for every successful union. Two neighbours from the same island would be subtracted twice.
Treating diagonal neighbours as connected, or forgetting the bounds check on the grid edges.

solutions.title: Flood fill after every operation
solutions.idea: Apply the fill, then count islands from scratch with BFS over the whole grid.

solutions.title: Union-find with a running count
solutions.idea: Each new cell adds one island; each union between two different roots removes one. Path compression and union by size make every step almost O(1).

followups: Cells can also turn back into water. Why does plain union-find stop working, and what could you do instead?
The grid is huge (10⁹ cells) but only 10⁴ cells ever become land. How do you store the parents?
